description: CADS-dataset is a large-scale collection of 22,022 CT volumes with voxel-level annotations covering 167 anatomical structures for whole-body CT segmentation. The dataset aggregates CT scans from over 40 diverse sources spanning more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, collected between 2007 and 2024. It includes both publicly sourced data and two newly contributed collections (484 head CTs and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans), covering a wide spectrum of clinical variability including healthy subjects and various pathological conditions.

name: CADS-dataset
rai:annotatorDemographics: Manual annotations were contributed by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist (Jan C. Peeken) for the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset. Expert review of test set annotations was performed by in-house medical professionals. Clinical evaluation was conducted by an experienced radiation oncologist with 5.5 years in practice. Labelata GmbH (Zurich, Switzerland) contributed to label quality review (Nikhil Mirajkar, Saad Khalid).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed through: (1) automated shape-based outlier detection using neural implicit functions, with the lowest-scoring 10% of pseudo-labels excluded based on 90th-percentile Hausdorff distance; (2) statistical flavor selection using Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Levene's variance equality tests, and ANOVA/Welch's ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis tests with post-hoc comparisons (Tukey's HSD or Dunn's test, p<0.05) to identify the best-performing annotation flavor per structure; (3) manual review of 65 test images from the TotalSegmentator dataset by in-house medical professionals, classifying each of 104 anatomical structure annotations as reliable or unreliable; (4) expert radiation oncologist review of segmentation quality on the real-world hospital cohort through systematic slice-by-slice review.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Annotations were generated using the nnU-Net framework for automated pseudo-labeling. Manual annotations were performed in-house by medical research assistants and radiation oncologists. Reference annotations for the real-world hospital cohort were generated using MIM software and validated by medical doctors or directly contoured by radiation oncologists.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A multi-stage annotation pipeline was used: (1) Pseudo-labeling: 167 target structures were organized into nine anatomical groups; specialized nnU-Net models were trained on high-quality annotations from established datasets and used to generate pseudo-labels across all 22,022 CT scans. (2) Shape-informed quality control: automated outlier detection using neural implicit functions and shape priors to filter unreliable pseudo-labels based on 90th-percentile Hausdorff distance. (3) Multi-strategy label optimization: three complementary model "flavors" (GT-flavor trained on ground truth, Pseudo-flavor trained on all pseudo-labels, Shape-flavor trained on quality-filtered pseudo-labels) were trained and statistically ranked per structure using Dice and HD95 metrics to select the best-performing annotation for each structure. (4) Final label assembly: best-performing flavor labels were merged with original GT annotations taking highest priority. Additional manual annotations were contributed by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist for the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset.
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges several potential biases: (1) Class imbalance: certain structures (e.g., uppermost cervical vertebrae C1-C5) appear less frequently across the 22,022 volumes, addressed through inverse-probability oversampling; (2) Shape-based quality control may exclude pathological cases with atypical anatomical variations, potentially limiting the model's ability to learn clinically important edge scenarios; (3) Approximately 79% of the initial collection lacks manual annotations, relying on pseudo-labels which can introduce noise and inaccuracies; (4) Facial features are intentionally anonymized due to privacy considerations, limiting applications requiring detailed facial analysis; (5) The data-centric approach using large-scale diverse data is explicitly designed to reduce variance-driven errors from boundary ambiguity, protocol heterogeneity, and inter-annotator inconsistency.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset aggregates CT scans from three main source categories: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator (1,203 annotated volumes), NLST (7,172 scans), CT-RATE (3,134 scans), and AbdomenCT-1K (1,062 scans); (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges (Grand Challenge, MICCAI) and focused research studies (Han-Seg, SAROS, TCIA oncology studies); and (3) newly contributed images comprising 484 anonymized head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar. Selection criteria focused on CT scans covering key anatomical regions throughout the body. The collection spans more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of volumetric CT scans in original image formats from 40 diverse sources. Of the 22,022 CT volumes, only 4,695 (approximately 21%) contain partial annotations from public sources; the remaining 79% have no annotations. The scans cover varying imaging protocols (contrast-enhanced and non-contrast acquisitions) and multiple anatomical regions (whole-body, head-and-neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, spine). Sources include public archives (TCIA, Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges) and hospital cohorts from over 100 medical centers across 16 countries.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Data collected between 2007 and 2024 across contributing institutions.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web API, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The paper identifies several limitations: (1) Shape-based quality control excludes pathological cases with atypical anatomical variations, limiting coverage of clinically important edge scenarios; (2) Coverage is limited to head-to-knee region; hands, feet, and finer vascular substructures are not included; (3) Several structures require refinement: brain mask is broadly defined including all CNS components within skull; optic chiasm tends to be under-segmented; heart segmentation omits superior portions; rectum appears shorter than anatomical extent; trachea limited to air content without surrounding cartilage wall; vena cava lacks anatomical precision; (4) Facial features are anonymized, limiting detailed facial analysis applications; (5) Some structures have limited training data (e.g., buccal mucosa appears in fewer than 1,000 scans with only 30 ground-truth annotations); (6) Very small organs (volumes below 0.5 mL) are challenging due to standard CT resolution limits and partial volume effects.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Several post-collection manipulations were applied: (1) Oversampling with inverse probability weights based on class occurrence frequency to address class imbalance (e.g., less frequent C1-C5 vertebrae received higher sampling weights); (2) Targeted training subsets for specialized anatomical regions (e.g., images with predicted brain voxel count >2,000 for brain group; at least 24 target structures for head-and-neck group); (3) Rib segmentation refinement: connected components analysis with majority voting for consistent rib labeling, and costovertebral joint retrieval using vesselFM with morphological opening and size filtering (100-1,500 voxels); (4) Head pseudo-label post-processing: quality control filter excluding scans with brain voxel count <2,000, and bounding box cropping to remove false positives outside head region; (5) SAROS sparse 2D slice annotations were interpolated to create dense 3D per-slice annotations.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-step standardization pipeline was applied: (1) reorientation of all images to the standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention; (2) resampling to a uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution to balance segmentation accuracy with computational efficiency; (3) simplification of original affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear. For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions to obscure identity while preserving structural integrity.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers. By making the dataset publicly available, the authors aim to accelerate innovation and promote AI adoption in medical image analysis. The dataset enables development of models for clinical applications including radiation oncology treatment planning, diagnostic radiology, and large-scale population studies. The open-source nature addresses accessibility barriers for healthcare practitioners without technical expertise. The dataset also contributes to addressing healthcare data challenges such as class imbalance and potential biases while reducing overfitting risks.
rai:dataUseCases: Intended use cases include: (1) Training and evaluation of whole-body CT segmentation models; (2) Radiation therapy planning through rapid organ delineation; (3) Diagnostic radiology for automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes; (4) Anatomical landmark detection for automated measurements; (5) Cross-modality registration for CT-MRI fusion and PET-CT alignment; (6) Anatomy-guided image reconstruction for radiation dose reduction; (7) Longitudinal organ tracking; (8) Personalized anatomical modeling; (9) Large-scale population studies; (10) Body composition analysis through tissue quantification; (11) Region-specific abnormality detection to support rapid diagnosis, triage, and mortality risk assessment.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net framework (version 2.5.1) was used for training specialized segmentation models and generating pseudo-labels. Neural implicit functions (auto-decoder based on implicit neural representations) were used for shape-based quality control of pseudo-labels. vesselFM (a foundation model for 3D blood vessel segmentation) was used to detect tubular structures for rib costovertebral joint retrieval. ANTs (Advanced Normalization Tools) non-rigid transformation was used for registering Han-Seg CT scans with the SimNIBS MRI atlas to generate brain structure annotations.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: All newly acquired hospital CT scans are anonymized. For the 484 head CT scans from Istanbul Medipol University, a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions to obscure patient identity. The study received ethical approval from two independent institutional review boards: the Clinical Research Ethics Committee at Istanbul Medipol University (E-10840098-772.02-6841, 27/10/2023) for the head CT scans, and the Ethics Committee of the Technical University of Munich (TUM) (27/19 S-SR) for the 586 abdominal CT scans. The dataset contains medical imaging data of patients with various pathological conditions.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a fixed number of independent annotations per item; annotations come from a mix of automated pseudo-labeling and selective manual annotation with no stated per-item annotation count.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling such as cloud filtering, missing timestamps, or incomplete records in the collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol for missing values is described; the paper uses pseudo-labeling to generate annotations for unlabeled scans rather than imputing missing data values.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
